19697-by-what-authority:
Great Keynes, a quiet backwater village, anchors the opening of By What Authority. A traveler waits there, impatient, while a horse is shod. London's whirl lies twenty miles north of him. The Brighton road rushes eight miles east. Against that stillness, the novel sets its question of authority. The story is a historical romance of England's religious struggles.

The famous tale behind this title concerns a young Catholic in Elizabethan England. Faith and crown pulled subjects in opposite directions then. A village far from court could still feel that pull. The novel uses slow country scenes to build its world. Its question, who may command belief, ran through the age.
20002-alroy-the-prince-of-the-captivity:
Benjamin Disraeli published Alroy in 1833, a romance of the medieval Jewish East. Its hero is David Alroy, the Prince of the Captivity. Disraeli defends his supernatural machinery as Cabalistically correct. From the Spirits of the Tombs to Solomon's sceptre, he claims Hebrew tradition as authority. The novel follows a would-be messiah raising revolt in Persia. Baghdad and the caliph's court frame his rising.

Disraeli, of Jewish descent, made Alroy his one Jewish epic. The historical Alroy led a twelfth-century movement among Kurdish Jews. Disraeli turns him into a Byronic conqueror-poet. Politics, prophecy, and ambition fuse in the hero exactly as in the author. Later prime ministers rarely leave juvenilia this revealing. Alroy is Disraeli dreaming his own destiny eastward.
20032-northern-nut-growers-report-of-the:
Northern nut growers met, spoke, and kept records of their meetings, and one such report survives here. The pages include long lists of members and guests. Names from Washington appear again and again in the roll. Karl W. Greene and T. P. Littlepage are among those listed.

Reports like this one record who came, where they lived, and what the group did. They are plain records, not tales, and their value lies in names and dates. Growers, officials, and keen amateurs all took part in this shared work on nuts and trees.
20160-a-history-of-american-christianity:
Leonard Woolsey Bacon published A History of American Christianity in 1897. Bacon was a minister and church historian of wide learning. He notes how near God's plans came to defeat by human enterprise. Medieval Norse trips to North America now look like fact, he argues.

From those early probes, the book traces churches across the new nation. Colonies, revivals, and new sects all pass in ordered review. Bacon writes as an insider who still weighs proof with care. Readers get a full, dated survey of faith in America to his day.
20174-freedom-truth-and-beauty:
Edward Doyle published Freedom, Truth, and Beauty in 1921, a book of poems and praise. Doyle was known as the blind poet of Harlem in New York. A note urges readers to take up his Haunted Temple poems. There they may feel shame for past moods of distrust and discontent.

His verse turns on faith, sight beyond eyes, and hope in hard life. Blindness shapes his image as a poet who sees by inner light. The book mixes his poems with warm words from his admirers. Readers get a period voice of faith and grit from Harlem's streets.
20337-a-narrative-of-the-mutiny-on-board:
William Bligh wrote A Narrative of the Mutiny on Board His Majesty's Ship Bounty. Bligh sailed from Otaheite on April 4, 1789, with his cargo safe. He carried 1,015 fine bread-fruit plants in the highest state of health. Many other valuable fruits of that country filled the ship too.

Weeks of care had gone into collecting those plants for transport. Weeks later, his crew rose and set him adrift in an open boat. Bligh's own account defends his conduct and tells that famed voyage home. Readers get the captain's voice from history's most famous mutiny.
20606-the-magic-city:
E. Nesbit's The Magic City is a children's fantasy about a boy who builds a city and steps inside it. Philip Haldane and his sister live in a little red-roofed house in a little red-roofed town. They have a little garden, a little balcony, and a little pony in a little stable.

When his sister marries and life changes, Philip builds a great model city from books, toys, and household things. The city becomes real, and Philip must rule and rescue it. Nesbit mixes everyday childhood with true wonder, in the style that made her the founder of modern children's fantasy.
20612-fort-amity:
Arthur Quiller-Couch set his novel Fort Amity in Canada during the French and Indian War. In his preface he hopes his remarks will not seem too pompous for the story he tells. It is a story in which true love is crossed by a soldier's sense of honor.

The theme, he admits, is a variant on a great commonplace. Following his habit, he lets the incidents and the characters make their own impression. Around the frontier fort, war between empires presses on private hearts. Quiller-Couch, who signed himself Q, writes the tale with a poet's care for place and speech.
20708-a-son-of-the-city:
Herman Gastrell Seely's A Son of the City, published in 1917, is a story of boy life in Chicago. Its hero grows up on city streets, with school, gangs, jobs, and baseball for his world. The first chapter's heading promises the pattern: In Which Our Hero Goes Fishing.

The book opens before dawn. Startled from a sound sleep, the boy fumbles beneath the bed to throttle the alarm clock. He must silence its clamor before it wakes the rest of the household. Seely writes city boyhood from the inside, in an age when such everyday stories for boys were rare.
20856-ten-from-infinity:
A Monarch Books science fiction novel from January 1963, Ten From Infinity bears Ivar Jorgensen's name. Ralph Brillhart painted its cover for the paperback trade. The imprint promised works picked for merit and reading fun alike.

Ten beings from beyond space give this brisk tale its hook and title. Paul Fairman, who wrote as Jorgensen, filled it with pulp pace and twists. Strange doubles and hidden foes drive the plot at speed. The book is a neat slice of early 1960s paperback science fiction, built to grip on the first page and not let go.
20936-the-new-society:
Ending the proletarian state can be neared, argues The New Society, by wise laws on property and schooling. Curbs on inheritance rights stand chief among its tools named here. Strict state control, the writer holds, is not required for that end.

Graham Wallas, a Fabian thinker, probes how great societies strain the human mind. Schools, wealth, and modern scale fill his thought on reform without revolt. Wallas wrote for readers who wanted reform. He asks how minds like ours can run states so vast. The book is a work of social thought.
20958-life-in-the-medieval-university:
Logic by Aristotle, sums by Boethius, and Euclid's geometry ruled the medieval schools, Robert S. Rait notes. Ptolemy stands for astronomy, though mixed with kings of his name. Theology crowned the long course that followed the arts degree.

Life in the Medieval University shows how scholars lived, ate, fought, and learned. Paris, Oxford, and Bologna supply tales of gowns, towns, and riots. Rait writes with a scholar's ease on a world half monkish, half rowdy. Students today will know much of it still: debt, lodging hunts, and fierce pride in one's own school and its ways.
21048-just-patty:
Mae Mertelle's financier father takes a hit from Patty Wyatt in Jean Webster's Just Patty, from 1911. Patty's own father, a reform judge, spends his days jailing financiers, she retorts. Her grin turns the proud boast into a shared schoolgirl laugh.

Patty, of Daddy-Long-Legs fame in Webster's wider world, stars in these school tales. Pranks, classes, and chums at St. Ursula's fill the brisk chapters. Webster writes girls with wit, nerve, and warm hearts in equal share. Just Patty shows her at her lightest, a convent school romp by a teller who never talked down to her girls.
21305-a-dash-from-diamond-city:
Two young men are sent from Mafeking with important despatches for the general at Kimberley in George Manville Fenn's Boer War tale. Their road crosses Boer-held country in South Africa, with mishaps at every stage. A side plot follows illicit diamond dealing around the diamond city of the title.

Just before reaching Kimberley the riders are badly wounded and lie unconscious for a fortnight. The despatches, sewn into a filthy, blood-stained jacket, are feared thrown away before they are found safe. Fenn opens in a mud-walled, iron-roofed office with typewriter and pens scratching, then moves out into the veld, where the dash is won or lost.
21772-the-path-of-duty:
An American long settled in London writes out a story for a curious friend in this Henry James tale of 1885. The story concerns Ambrose Tester, and the narrator knew all the parties from the first. He promises a regular development and tells it by a red fire in the December fog. Sixteen years of London life have left him, he says, still sensitive to the city's strangeness.

The title names the tale's pressure: what people owe, and what owing costs them. James builds the story from observation, talk, and small social turns rather than big events. London's bigness and strangeness fill the frame. It is James in his early manner, a moral knot tied slowly in good company.
21839-sense-and-sensibility:
Two sisters stand at the heart of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility, shown here in the 1902 Macmillan edition. One sister is ruled by sense, the other by feeling. Hugh Thomson's drawings, first issued in 1896, fill this printing. The Dashwoods have long been settled at Norland Park in Sussex when the tale begins. A death soon strips the family of home and income, and the sisters must make their way in a narrower world.

Elinor hides her heart while Marianne wears hers openly, and love tests both habits hard. Austen writes courtship as a study in character, with wit in every drawing room. Austin Dobson supplies the introduction. It is Austen's first published novel, and still one of her most loved.
21960-blue-bonnet-s-ranch-party:
A Texas girl takes her friends west in Blue Bonnet's Ranch Party, part of the Blue Bonnet series for girls, issued in 1912. Blue Bonnet's party rides in a private car and still finds the journey to Woodford the longest-seeming ever taken. The frontispiece watches her see the sun rise out of the prairie. Lela Horn Richards and Caroline E. Jacobs created the series, with this sequel written by C. E. Jacobs and Edyth Ellerbeck.

The series ran through Boston, housekeeping, and a debut before and after this ranch visit. Thirteen impressions by 1921 show how girls loved her. John Goss drew the pictures. The book gives its heroine both worlds: Boston polish and a Texas ranch, with the ranch winning the party's heart.
21981-the-essentials-of-spirituality:
What spirituality is, apart from any creed, is Felix Adler's question in The Essentials of Spirituality. Adler, founder of the Ethical Culture movement, begins with hunger: first the felt absence of spirituality, then the search for a higher quality of life. The quality, he argues, may come through belief in a divine father, through Spinoza's pantheism, through Buddhism's Nirvana, or through Ethical Culture itself.

He warns that the word spiritual often serves as a synonym for muddy thought and misty feeling. His remedy is definition joined to portraits of character. The essay is short, calm, and meant for seekers outside the churches. It shows Adler's lifelong project: keeping the moral fire of religion while letting its doctrines go. Few American sermons argue so gently.
22118-official-report-of-the-niger-valle:
Martin R. Delany, a Black abolitionist, doctor, and writer, led an exploring party to West Africa in 1859. His Official Report of the Niger Valley Exploring Party argues the case for emigration. Delany held that Black Americans must win a place of entire equality somewhere. He looked to the Niger valley as a land where a rising generation could rule itself.

The report describes the country, its peoples, its cotton, and its trade. It also answers critics of the emigration plan in strong terms. Delany's mission signed a treaty with Yoruba leaders for settlement land. The document stands as a founding text of Black nationalism, written before the Civil War freed the enslaved.
22239-security:
Security is a science fiction tale of a regimented future and a man saving for escape. Its Lancaster has two assets: his savings and an extra liquor ration. Tonight, coming home through the tube, he decides to make a dent in the whiskey. He ate at the commissary as usual but skipped the talk, thinking of the drink all the way home.

That small rebellion opens a story about control, rationing, and the price of safety. The future here runs on commissary meals, tubes, and allotted pleasures. Pulp writers used such sketches to test how much freedom men trade for security. The tale's chill comes from its quietness: nothing explodes, yet everything is owned.
22585-and-devious-the-line-of-duty:
And Devious the Line of Duty is a science fiction story of war and alliance among future worlds. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its politics turn on Jardeen, a large companion world whose space navy outmatches that of any other single world.

Neutral worlds wait to follow Jardeen's lead, so its choice of allies may decide a war. An alliance between Jardeen and the Verdam People's Worlds would, the narrator warns, quickly end the Terran Republic. The stakes are set out in the clipped style of pulp space opera. Readers who like grand strategy, rival star nations, and old magazine science fiction will find a compact example of the form.
22623-divinity:
Divinity is a science fiction story of a man adrift in space, weighing a desperate escape. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its hero, cut off from his ship and crew, thinks wildly for a moment before the risks of freedom in space come clear to him.

He must reach a civilized port, persuade the authorities he was shipwrecked and parted from his crew, then vanish into the crowd. The dangers are plain, but he takes them: anything beats running out of air and food alone in the dark. The story wrings tension from logistics and loneliness rather than monsters. It is a lean example of the stranded-spaceman tale from the magazine years.
23067-stories-of-animal-sagacity:
Cats and dogs open Stories of Animal Sagacity. The author begins with anecdotes of the sagacity shown by animals all readers know well. Anyone who watches a pet closely, the author says, will recognize the behavior. Readers will think of their own Tabby's tricks, or of a dog at home who once did nearly as clever a thing.

Anecdote follows anecdote, horses, elephants, birds, and more joining the cats and dogs. Each story argues that animals reason, remember, and feel more than people grant. Victorian natural history loved such collections, halfway between science and fireside wonder. The book's charm is its faith in close watching. It invites young readers to test every claim against the pet asleep by their own chair.
23290-the-dogs-dinner-party:
The Dog's Dinner Party is a story told through animals. One guest, a dog charged with watching over and protecting the livestock, fears he must decline his invitation. On second thoughts, he resolves to venture out anyway, since it is not a late dinner.

He can get away early, he reckons. His coat is rather the worse for wear, which troubles him. But he does own one handsome collar, at least. So he accepts. Readers get a genteel animal tale that plays human manners for gentle comedy: duty, dress, and dinner invitations, all weighed by a conscientious dog.
a-beleaguered-city:
Margaret Oliphant, a Scots writer of great range, wrote this strange tale of a French town in 1880. The town is Semur, a quiet place of old homes and slow days. Oliphant was famed for sober tales of real life, which makes this book stand out.

The dead of the town rise and come back, in a calm and grave host. They drive the living from their homes, yet do no harm and speak no word that men can grasp. The tale's power lies in its hush: a siege by ghosts, told with rare weight and calm.
a-woman-of-thirty:
Honoré de Balzac begins on a bright Sunday morning in April 1813, in Ellen Marriage's translation, as a worried father hands his beautiful young daughter down from a carriage in Paris. The first part, called Early Mistakes, follows her into a marriage chosen for rank rather than love. Her life becomes the book's long study.

In linked episodes Balzac follows the woman through young love, boredom, a lover, children, loss, and age, watching how each stage changes her heart. an-exhortation-to-peace-and-unity:
John Bunyan's treatise takes its text from Ephesians: endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. An editorial note in this 1845 printing admits the work's genuineness has been questioned, yet prints it with the collected works, as most editions do. The voice that speaks is Bunyan's in manner, plain and urgent.

Religion, the treatise argues, is the great bond of human society, and it shames Christians when religion itself is split by strife. The writer pleads with believers who hold one Lord, one faith, and one baptism to stop wounding each other over lesser things. The tract is short, warm, and practical, aimed at church quarrels of Bunyan's own hard century.
b09-luther-address-nobility:
Martin Luther aimed his 1520 address, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, straight at the princes of Germany. He argued that Rome had built three walls to guard its power from reform. Behind them, Rome claimed that church rule outranks earthly rule. It claimed that only Rome can read Scripture, and only the pope can call a council.

Luther knocks down each wall in turn and calls on the nobility to act. The address gave the Reformation a clear public program, in German, for lay rulers to carry out. It also stands as a founding text of German national feeling. Few pamphlets of the age reached so far.
b09-luther-babylonian-captivity:

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:

govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_President_Tr:

jukes-edwards-a-study-in-education-and-h:

luther-concerning-christian-liberty:
Two sentences state the whole Reformation in Luther's Concerning Christian Liberty, from 1520. A Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none; a Christian is a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. The treatise, read here in the Wace and Buchheim translation, unfolds that paradox.

Faith frees the believer from earning God's favor, and that freedom then spends itself in love of neighbor. Works follow faith as fruit follows a living tree, never the other way round. Luther lays out justification by faith with unmatched clarity and warmth. The little book served as the movement's charter in miniature. New readers still start with it, and old hands return to it.
mill-on-liberty:
John Stuart Mill published On Liberty in 1859, the classic defense of free thought and free lives. Mill wrote it with his wife Harriet Taylor Mill, whose part he praised in the warmest terms. The essay is short, calm, and built like a proof.

Mill lays down one rule: power may limit a person's freedom only to stop harm to others. On that base he defends free speech even for false views, since truth grows stronger by meeting error. He also guards the space for odd, bold experiments in living. The essay still anchors arguments on speech and liberty everywhere.

nasa-tm-19650014965-measurement-relation:

From that base, a likely source direction and a flux correction factor can be worked out. The relationships turn raw puncture counts into a more honest measure of the hazard.
nasa-tm-19660010472-numerical-procedures:

nasa-tm-19660021038-the-spectral-distrib:
Steve Alexander, in the Radiometry Group of Goddard's Spacecraft Technology Division, measured the light of a carbon arc in March 1966. A carbon arc is a bright lamp made by an electric spark between carbon rods. Labs used it as a standard light source for testing instruments. Alexander reports how its energy is spread across wavelengths, and how even that spread is across the lamp's face.

A standard source is useful only if its output is known and steady. Spectral distribution tells users how much light falls in each color band. Uniformity tells them whether the bright spot can be trusted as even. Radiometry, the science of measuring light, rests on standards checked in exactly this careful way.

nasa-tm-19690010266-investigation-of-a-d:
Major Clinton Lee investigated a dual resonant cavity absorption cell in this master's thesis at the University of Virginia, dated August 1968. The cell serves double-resonance microwave spectroscopy, a method that identifies gases by the exact microwave bands they absorb. Two linked absorptions in one gas sample are watched at once, each in its own cavity.

Each cavity is a Fabry-Perot interferometer, and the two sit at right angles inside one vacuum enclosure. Separate microwave sources excite them, and Lee tracks how one transition's signal varies with pressure, power, and cavity quality. His test gas was methylene chloride. The measured sensitivity, he reports, matches conventional Stark modulated spectrometers, with gains expected at higher frequencies.
nasa-tm-19720004195-what-can-nuclear-ene:

Rom surveyed the uses then foreseen for nuclear energy. Electric power production led the list, with transportation methods close behind. He judged future needs and the likely impact of wider use. His conclusion, per the catalog record, was firm. Society would come to need nuclear power in many forms, he concluded.

painted-windows-studies-in-religious-per:
Painted Windows: Studies in Religious Personality appeared in 1922 under a mask. Its author signed himself only A Gentleman with a Duster. He had written The Mirrors of Downing Street under the same name. The studies portray English religious leaders of the day. Bishop Gore fronts the book as its frontispiece. Professor Kirsopp Lake wrote the introduction.

Lake takes the portraits seriously. The churches, he says, were once the moral leaders of western civilization. The book warns that the Church is failing in that role. The failure is not from lack of earnestness. Today's guides are serious, upright men. They would gladly lead if they could. Lake's question — why they cannot — frames every portrait that follows.
philosophy-4-a-story-of-harvard-universi:
Owen Wister's Philosophy 4, a story of Harvard University, opens on a sweltering May night in Cambridge. Two boys in tennis flannels sit cramming for an examination, gloomy under lamp and gas. A tutor drones through the Absolute Intelligence and the Cogito while the Mephistopheles clock on the shelf strikes eleven.

The boys suck their pencils, scrawl notes, and beg him to skip Plato, whose points they got yesterday. Wister, who wrote The Virginian, turns from the West to his own college. The story catches wealthy undergraduates, hired coaches, and the terror of a philosophy examination at the old Harvard.
pillars-of-society:
Henrik Ibsen's Pillars of Society, a play in four acts translated by R. Farquharson Sharp, is set in a smaller coast town in Norway. The action takes place at the house of Karsten Bernick, a shipbuilder whose family and business stand at the center of town life.

Around Bernick gather his wife, their thirteen-year-old son Olaf, his sister Martha, and his wife's brother Johan Tonnesen and half-sister Lona Hessel. The household also shelters Dina Dorf, a young girl living with the family, while merchants, tradesmen, and Bernick's clerk and yard foreman fill out the town. In four acts Ibsen tests the respectability of a man the town treats as one of its pillars.
podcast-joerogan-3SpWWU5O8TY:
Where does drive end and addiction begin? A segment of the Joe Rogan Experience takes up that line, with Rogan thinking out loud about training, work, and habits that can own a person. Rogan built his career on obsessive effort, which makes the question personal.

The talk tests the same hunger in two lights: as the engine of a strong life and as a trap that shrinks it. Rogan weighs gym habits, creative work, and the pull of substances, asking how you can tell when want turns into need. It is a plain-spoken hour on self-control, reward, and knowing when to stop.
podcast-joerogan-7ph99mEQrTY:
Journalist Michael Shellenberger joins Joe Rogan for episode 2465 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Shellenberger wrote Apocalypse Never against climate alarm and later reported on the censorship files from inside Twitter's records. His work bridges energy, cities, and free speech fights.

Shellenberger lays out his case against the green machine and the policies he says hurt the poor. He describes what the internal files showed about government pressure on platforms. Rogan asks about his run-ins with the activists and officials he criticizes. Questioning and green-skeptical listeners get the author in full, long form.
pressure-resistance-and-stability-of-ear:
J. C. Meem presented this paper to the American Society of Civil Engineers as Paper Number 1174 of its Transactions, on the pressure, resistance, and stability of earth. The subject is the ground itself as an engineering material: how hard soil pushes against trenches, tunnels. Retaining structures, how piles and foundations resist, and how underwater structures in soft ground bear pressure and buoyancy. Meem returns to his earlier paper on bracing trenches with new, larger experiments on the arching properties of sand.

His first experiment builds a sand box three feet wide with wooden abutments and a sliding false bottom, big enough, he argues, to answer critics of small-scale tests. Discussion by seven engineers is printed with the paper. The document preserves foundation engineering when earth pressure was still settled by sandbox and argument.
psmith-in-the-city:
P. G. Wodehouse sent his two school friends into the business world in a comic novel where Mike faces bad news at home and Psmith talks his way through every fix. Mr. Bickersdyke, a bank manager and would-be member of Parliament, becomes their chief trial.

Chapter titles promise first steps in a business career, winter quarters, stirring times on the common, and a discovery made by Psmith. Cricket, banking, and local politics collide as the pair keep their nerve and their manners. Readers get early Wodehouse: calm, absurd talk laid over a plot of money and reputation.
raphael-or-pages-of-the-book-of-life-at-:
Raphael, or Pages of the Book of Life at Twenty, is by Alphonse de Lamartine. It appears here in an illustrated edition of the Société des Beaux-Arts. The edition is dated Paris, London, and New York, 1905. It belongs to the Comédie d'Amour series. Its pictures are by Sandoz. An opening essay, Lamartine and His Writings, tells the poet's life before the tale begins.

Lamartine was born at Mâcon on October 21, 1790, taught by his mother, and schooled at Belley. At Aix he met Madame Charles. She died in 1817. Their love, the essay says, forms the basis of Raphael. The book is one of the purest and most delicate sentiment. His Méditations Poétiques followed in 1820.
safe-marriage-a-return-to-sanity: Ettie A. Rout wrote Safe Marriage, A Return to Sanity, issued in London in 1922 by William Heinemann (Medical Books) Ltd. A preface by Sir William Arbuthnot Lane, consulting surgeon to Guy's Hospital, is named on the title page. A portrait of Rout, by Vandyk of London, faces the title. The pages shown here also carry a publisher's notice for a separate work on prevention of venereal disease by Sir Archdall Reid, with praise quoted from the Lancet and the Medical Press.
sidelights-on-relativity:
Albert Einstein delivered the two addresses in this small volume to learned audiences in Europe. The first, on ether and the theory of relativity, was given at the University of Leyden on May 5, 1920. The second treats geometry and experience, in a fuller form of a Berlin academy address from January 27, 1921.

Einstein asks why physicists kept faith in an ether beside solid matter. Action at a distance and the wave theory of light supply his answer's roots. Readers meet relativity from its maker's own mouth, in talks meant for scholars yet famed for their clarity of thought.
steam-steel-and-electricity:
James W. Steele tells three tales of making in Steam, Steel and Electricity, and the contents lay out each in fine detail. The Story of Steam runs from what steam is and steam in nature through the Hero engine and the temple-door machine. Savery's and Papin's engines follow, then Watt's gains on the Newcomen plan, the crank, the governor, and the first engine by an American maker.

The Age of Steel takes up the ages of man's making, bronze, and what steel is. Lost arts, eastern steel, cast steel, and the first iron finds and works in America lead to the trip-hammer, Nasmyth's steam-hammer, rolling mills, and the Bessemer process and its converter. The Story of Electricity, called the oldest and youngest of the sciences, starts with the origin of its name and old ideas about it.
the-abominations-of-modern-society:
Rev. T. De Witt Talmage, author of Crumbs Swept Up, published The Abominations of Modern Society in 1872, a set of stern talks on the vices of city life. His preface, signed at Brooklyn on January 1, 1872, frames the book as a warning buoy.

Talmage calls the book a buoy swung over rocks, meant to keep any craft from a lee shore on its last day out. He says it speaks to young and old, men and women alike. Listed talks take on winter nights, the power of clothes, late hours, dance, sweatshop sewing, lewd papers, and club houses. Readers get a famed preacher's blunt tour of Gilded Age temptations.
the-argonauts-of-north-liberty:
Bret Harte sets this tale in North Liberty, Connecticut, a town he calls cheerless on any day and bleakest on the Sabbath. Part One opens as the bell of the Second Presbyterian Church stops ringing on a chilly March evening in 1850. Sleet and hail spit in the faces of churchgoers fighting their way to the door.

Inside, the rigor peaks: shivering gas-jets light bare walls and hard-set faces under drawn curtains. Harte paints a town sealed against kindliness, where even the Sabbath sun gives up and stares in stony wonder. That frozen piety is the ground against which his Argonauts, gold seekers in spirit, will soon stand out.
the-bacillus-of-beauty:
Harriet Stark called her book a romance of to-day and built its contents around a girl's change in looks. Early book headings name a broken chrysalis, a change, and the most beautiful woman in the world. A hornet's nest, a goddess and a mob, and a concert follow.

Later books track a quest for knowledge, a girl bachelor and a biologist, and the finding of the bacillus named in the title. Love enters, then Christmas, reporters, and a council rock scene appear in the headings. A final book, called the bruising of the wings, hints that sudden beauty brings trouble as well as joy.
the-basis-of-morality:
Annie Besant published a study at Adyar, Madras, in 1915 with the Theosophical Publishing House. Five chapters name five proposed grounds for right and wrong: revelation, intuition, utility, evolution, and mysticism. Besant is also listed for books on mysticism and the perfecting of man.

She opens by asking whether religion and morals must go together, and whether one can be taught without the other. France, she says, tried a dry catechism that made boys long to be wicked. Her real question is plainer: what firm base can tell right from wrong and stand against the storms of life? Each chapter tests one answer.
the-blue-bird-for-children-the-wonderful: Georgette Leblanc wrote The Blue Bird for Children, a school book drawn from the tale of Tyltyl and Mytyl and their search for joy. Frederick Orville Perkins edited and set it up for schools, and Alexander Teixeira de Mattos made the English text. Silver, Burdett and Company of Boston, New York, and Chicago put it out, with rights dated 1913 and 1914. The front pages name the two young seekers and the theme of the quest, but they give no part of the tale itself.
the-bobbsey-twins-in-a-great-city: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins in a Great City, put out in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. The front pages place it ninth in her Bobbsey set. The earlier tales are set in the country, at the shore, at school, and at Snow Lodge. Others sit on a houseboat, at Meadow Brook, and at home. A front plate shows the young folk glad at a camp set up in a shop. No part list or tale page is shown.
the-boy-scouts-on-picket-duty:
Scout Master Robert Shaler wrote The Boy Scouts on Picket Duty. Its chapters start with a strange steamer and a cargo of banned goods. A lone scout, a hut on the beach, and a kidnapping by smugglers come next. The flight of the Arrow, a clan gathering, and a blazing beacon lead to the end of the raid.

The tale opens in the wake of a squall, off Snipe Point in Florida Bay, near Key West. The sloop Arrow, owned and sailed by Lemuel Vinton, runs south with all sails hauled tight. She bears a startling message, one her captain holds grave enough to cut short his cruise and hurry back to port. Her crew is five Boy Scouts, an older hand in charge, and Dave, a Seminole guide hired for a short trip into the Everglades. Hugh Hardin, Billy Worth, and Chester Brownell are named among the boys.
the-diary-of-a-man-of-fifty:
Henry James's The Diary of a Man of Fifty opens in Florence on April 5th, 1874. The diarist has been told he would find Italy greatly changed, and in twenty-seven years there is room for changes. To him, though, all is so perfectly the same that he seems to be living his youth over again, its forgotten impressions rushing back.

He compares those impressions to lines written in sympathetic ink. They are brought out when the letter is held to the fire: the yellow sun of Florence has restored the text of his own young romance. At fifty-two, with fair health, a fair fortune, and a tidy conscience, he supposes he is bound to write himself happy, yet he shirks the duty. He has not been miserable, but positive happiness would have been different, and he turns back to a buried episode of more than a quarter-century ago.
the-eternal-city:
Hall Caine's The Eternal City, copyrighted in 1901 and 1902, opens with a prologue in London. A boy of ten or twelve, in rags, bears an accordion in a case on one shoulder and a caged grey squirrel under the other arm, on a December night. He seems scarce fit, the tale says, to figure in the great review of life.

That boy grows into a plot of Rome, revolution, and love. Caine, who wrote The Christian, sets a foundling's rise against the Vatican and the people's hopes. A scripture line heads the book: a city whose builder is God.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-i-the-man-of-pro: John Galsworthy wrote The Man of Property as volume one of The Forsyte Saga. This copy's heading dates it 1906. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. The first heads name an at home at Old Jolyon's. They name a dinner at Swithin's and plans of the house. June's treat and a drive with Swithin follow. Soames and Bosinney write to each other. No page of the novel itself appears in these opening pages.
the-foundations-of-personality: Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here, before the book itself begins. It names The Foundations of Personality by Abraham Myerson. It gives the book's release data from December 1998. No title page follows in the pages given here. No contents list or chapter text can be read either. So nothing about the author's views on character and mind can be told from these opening pages alone.
the-growth-of-thought-as-affecting-the-p: William Withington wrote The Growth of Thought as Affecting the Progress of Society. The book is dated 1851. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a full contents list in four parts. Part I defines life and takes up self-love and three agencies for bettering the human condition. Part II treats welfare as resting on social institutions, and names the Papacy's political fault. Part III makes philosophy the educator of self-love. Part IV turns to religion. A conclusion gives suggestions to Christian ministers.
the-history-of-the-fabian-society: Edward R. Pease wrote The History of the Fabian Society. He was secretary of the Society for twenty-five years. E. P. Dutton & Company published the book in New York. It carries twelve illustrations. The contents summarize chapters in detail. Chapter one treats the sources of Fabian socialism. It reaches back to the ideas of the early eighties. Chapter two treats the foundations of the Society in 1883-4. Chapter three treats the early days, when Bernard Shaw joined. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-jewel-city:
Ben Macomber wrote this guide to San Francisco's great fair. The Panama-Pacific fair of 1915 is its subject. A colored frontispiece fronts the book. More than seventy-five other pictures fill it. His opening takes a visitor's cry in the Fine Arts hall. All the beauty of the world had been sifted, the visitor said. The finest of it stood gathered here.

Macomber argues the fair set a new mark. Older fairs ordered each hall from a lone designer. Each worked apart from the rest. Artists came late to soften the clashes. San Francisco bound its halls to one shared theme. The theme was joy at the Panama Canal's completion. Courts, towers, and arches carried it in symbols. Planning, music, gardens, and exhibits fill his pages.
the-ladies-a-shining-constellation-of-wi:
E. Barrington's preface to these stories of famous women states her method honestly. Historical exactness is not the aim, she says. Unbending accuracy in dates is not either. She re-creates the personalities of charming women instead. The line runs from Elizabeth Pepys to Fanny Burney. Elizabeth was the diarist's wife. Fanny stood at Queen Charlotte's court. Much is imagination and more is truth, Barrington admits. Which is which she scarcely can tell herself.

She poses the questions her tales answer in fancy. What would Elizabeth Pepys have felt reading the Diary's secrets? What if Swift's Stella and Vanessa had met? Was there no finer touch in Elizabeth Gunning's stolen marriage? Horace Walpole's gossip records little else. Elizabeth Bennet, who never lived, is the most real of all. Barrington keeps her as a shadow in the background. She is not touched directly.
the-lady-of-big-shanty:
F. Berkeley Smith published this Adirondack novel in 1909. A prefatory note by his father explains its theme. F. Hopkinson Smith signed it in September 1909. The theme is the power of the primeval over the human mind. Once a man is abandoned in the wilderness, standards collapse. He depends on what can be wrested from nature's clutch. Neither love, money, nor social success brings a cup of water. No coal of fire comes from them either.

Under that torture, nature becomes king and man an atom. His judgment clarifies and his soul turns inside out. Chapter One opens far from the woods. It is the luncheon hour at The Players club in New York. Actors and professional men crowd the room. Tobacco smoke, pewter, and laughter fill it. The contrast is the novel's engine. Clubland ease will soon meet Big Shanty and the wilderness.
the-little-colonel-s-house-party: The Little Colonel's House Party by Annie Fellows Johnston was issued in Boston by L. C. Page and Company in 1907, illustrated by Louis Meynell. Only the title page and the publisher's list of Johnston's works are present here, so the story itself does not appear. That list presents the Little Colonel Series volume by volume, pricing The Little Colonel Stories at $1.50 and naming earlier titles such as Two Little Knights of Kentucky and The Story of Dago.
the-lost-city:
Joseph E. Badger, Jr. wrote The Lost City, a thirty-two-chapter adventure built around a character called Professor Featherwit. The contents promise a tornado ride, a duel to the death, and a marvelous vision. Then they reach the heart of the book: The Lost City of the Aztecs and its people, the Children of the Sun God. Later chapters put the professor before the gods, beneath a sacrificial stone, and defending the Sun Children against overwhelming odds. Chapter one, Nature in Travail, opens with a tiny exchange.

A voice says, "I say, professor?" The professor answers, "Very well, Waldo; proceed." From that small start, the contents map a lost-world adventure of exploration, danger, and rescue, ending with an adieu to the lost city.
the-national-being-some-thoughts-on-an-i:
The National Being, subtitled Some Thoughts on an Irish Polity, is signed A.E., the pen name of George William Russell, and dedicated to Sir Horace Plunkett. The dedication letter jokes about Plunkett's grafting, years earlier, of a slip of poetry onto his economic tree. This book, Russell says, is the hybrid result. It is not economics in Plunkett's sense, and not poetry in Russell's. Plunkett therefore bears responsibility for it.

Chapter I opens in 1914, amid world conflict, with the announced birth of the infant State of Ireland. The birth went almost unnoticed while Mars, the red planet of war, was ascendant. Russell pictures the child hidden away like Hercules in his cradle, with twin serpents of sectarianism ready to strangle it unless its guardians watched.
the-one-great-reality: Louisa Clayton, author of Heart Lessons and other devotional books, gathered her addresses under the title The One Great Reality. She dedicated the book to her friends in Rusthall, recalling thirty years of fellowship in the gospel, and Evan H. Hopkins wrote the foreword. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here, so the addresses themselves do not appear. The contents begin with God, the Great Reality, and God, Our Father.
the-penalty: Gouverneur Morris published The Penalty in 1913, illustrated by Howard Chandler Christy. Only the front matter is present here, a long dedication letter to Mary Baldwin, so the novel itself does not appear. Morris tells her that if her part of his life were lost, only a skeleton would remain. He recalls an Iliad she wrote and he drew as children, riding over old battlefields together, and a Colt revolver that shot a buffalo from a train. The letter is a memoir in miniature.
the-prince-and-betty: P. G. Wodehouse's The Prince and Betty, in its American edition of 1912, is shown through its contents. The chapters themselves are not on view. The list opens with The Cable from Mervo and Mervo and Its Owner. Vive le Roi follows, then Mr. Scobell Has Another Idea and Young Adam Cupid. An Ultimatum from the Throne and Mervo Changes Its Constitution raise the stakes. Later entries include Peaceful Moments, Betty Makes a Friend, A Change of Policy, and The First Battle.
the-psychology-of-beauty: Ethel D. Puffer's The Psychology of Beauty is identified in its Project Gutenberg header as Etext 3751, released in February 2003 and first posted in August 2001. The header notes the file was prepared by Tony Adam. The pages provided consist of that old-style header alone, with its copyright cautions and appeal for donations. Puffer's chapters on the psychology of aesthetic experience do not appear in the pages at hand.
the-rustlers-of-pecos-county:
Zane Grey published The Rustlers of Pecos County in 1914, and its first chapter is headed Vaughn Steele and Russ Sittell. The narrator, the cowboy Russ, tells the story in the first person from the town of Sanderson.

After an early breakfast Russ walks the main street gathering observations and information likely to serve him later, then returns to the hotel. George Wright pays him off with money from Miss Sampson, saying she will not need him at the ranch any more and that he need not speak with her. The girls then appear and greet Russ warmly, in a manner Wright cannot help but see, undercutting the dismissal.
the-secret-city:
Hugh Walpole published The Secret City with George H. Doran Company in New York in 1919. He dedicated it to Major James Annand, in return for the gift of his friendship. An ancient Cock-Crow Song serves as epigraph. The novel falls into three parts, named for Vera and Nina, Lawrence, and Markovitch and Semyonov.

The narrator opens by sorting through a bundle of manuscript. No writer ever fulfils his intention, he says. He had meant to keep himself outside the story entirely. Seeing Russian psychology through English eyes is the book's only excuse, he argues. Of Russia and the Russians he knows nothing, he confesses. He knows something of their effect on his own ideas during three years. The facts are true, he claims, while the inferences are absolutely his own.
the-story-of-electricity:
John Munro, author of Heroes of the Telegraph, wrote this popular account of electricity, and his preface of July 1915 argues that knowledge of electrical principles should belong to everyone's mental equipment. Stop all electrical service suddenly, he says, and anyone would feel how large a factor it is in daily comfort, industrial organization, and civilization itself.

The book presents the main facts in a popular way. It begins with where electrical energy comes from. Friction, chemical action, heat, and magnetism are its sources. The main discussion covers the nineteenth century's services: electroplating, telegraph, telephone and wireless, light and heat, power transmission, and transport. A publishers' note adds that this edition alters terminology to American usage and adds new matter and illustrations.
the-texan-star-the-story-of-a-great-figh: The Texan Star, Joseph A. Altsheler's story of a great fight for liberty, was published in New York in 1912. Title page and a full contents list are what this record offers, with no chapter text following. Twenty chapters run from prisoners and a hair-cut through a dungeon under the sea, a black jaguar, ruined temples, and a long chase, ending with the wheel of fire. The list maps a boy's adventure across Texas and Mexico in wartime, but Altsheler's scenes themselves are not shown.
the-vertical-city:
Fannie Hurst, author of Humoresque and Gaslight Sonatas, published her story collection The Vertical City in 1922. Contents pages list six pieces: She Walks in Beauty, Back Pay, the title story, The Smudge, Guilty, and Roulette. The first story opens inside the Bon Ton hotel, a fourteen-storey pile of elegantly furnished suites.

Hurst compares the hotel to the Taj Mahal, raised by grief for a dead wife and a cold hearthstone. The Bon Ton is likewise a mausoleum to the hearth, a tomb to Hestia in Indiana limestone and Vermont marble. At sixty dollars a week and up, guests leave the language of the fireside chair behind at the door.
three-acres-and-liberty: Bolton Hall, author of Things As They Are and Thrift, published Three Acres and Liberty with Macmillan in New York. Copyright dates of 1907 and 1918 mark this revised edition, reprinted many times before revision in February 1918. An epigraph compares a sower to a man sowing what is in his heart. A foreword heading follows the title pages, but its text does not appear in what is present. Readers can identify Hall's back-to-the-land book and its edition history, while Hall's advice itself is not shown here.
twenty:
Stella Benson's Twenty, dated 1918, gathers twenty poems, following her novels This Is the End and I Pose. The contents open with Christmas, 1917 and close with New Year, 1918. Songs, an orchard piece, a dog called Tupman, and a Cornishman stand between those wartime markers.

The first poem asks whether a faery door and golden palace can survive the present cruel age. Has the past died, the speaker wonders, or has the immortal Day only been stoned to martyrdom? Spring rain, summer, and autumn's burning carry the answer forward. Benson writes wartime verse that holds private gladness against public grief.
two-years-in-the-forbidden-city:
Princess Der Ling's Two Years in the Forbidden City rests on her post as first lady in waiting to the Empress Dowager. A foreword builds her credentials through her father, Lord Yu Keng. He served against the Taiping, fought in the Formosan war with France, and later represented China in Japan and France.

Yu Keng educated his daughters abroad, then almost unheard of for a high Manchu official, and attempts were made to impeach him as pro-foreign. Der Ling finished school at a French convent and entered society before returning to court. Her engagement to an American, Thaddeus C. White, ended her court connection in 1907. The foreword promises an intimate portrait of the woman who ruled China.
un-doc-declaration-on-world-food-securit:
The Declaration on World Food Security came from a high-level meeting in Rome on 5 June 2008. Leaders from 181 countries gathered at the call of the Food and Agriculture Organization. Food prices had soared across the world that year. Climate change and fuel crops pressed on supplies from the other side.

The text calls 862 million hungry people a fact no one can accept. It renews the 1996 pledge to halve hunger by 2015. Donors must fund quick food aid and safety nets now. Small farmers need seed, feed, and tools to grow more. For the long run, farm science and fairer trade get the stress. Fuel crops must be weighed with care.
un-doc-draft-united-nations-guiding-prin:
The Draft Guiding Principles on Human Rights and Extreme Poverty were approved by the United Nations Sub-Commission on Human Rights on 24 August 2006. Deep poverty lasts in rich and poor lands alike. A UN expert group had shaped the draft over years. People living in poverty spoke at the work sessions themselves.

The draft calls poverty a lasting lack of means, choices, safety, and power. Deep poverty and being shut out of society breach human dignity, it says. The poor hold every human right in full. They must help shape all plans that touch their lives. States, firms, and aid bodies must act on clear, open lines and answer for the results.
un-doc-moon-treaty:
The Moon Treaty, adopted by the United Nations in 1979, sets rules for states acting on the Moon and other bodies in space. Its full title speaks of governing the activities of states beyond Earth. Few major space powers ever ratified it, which makes the text a record of an road not taken.

The treaty declares the Moon and its resources the common heritage of all mankind. It calls for an international system to share any gains from lunar mining. It also bars weapons and military bases. Readers get the full legal vision states debated, then mostly set aside.
un-un-res-draft-united-nations-guiding-p:
Extreme poverty is treated as a human rights problem in these draft guiding principles, prepared for the United Nations in 2006. Standard rights texts rarely named poverty itself as a breach. The draft tries to close that gap by stating what states owe to people living in deep poverty.

The principles link poverty to blocked access to food, housing, health care, and schooling. They demand that poor people take part in decisions that affect them. They also call for aid duties across borders. The draft fed into later UN work that framed poverty as a rights issue, not just bad luck.
un-un-res-un-declaration-on-sexual-orien:
Gay rights reached the floor of the United Nations in this 2008 declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity. Dozens of states backed the text, which was read out in the General Assembly. It was the first UN statement devoted to the rights of gay, lesbian, and trans people.

The declaration condemns violence, torture, and criminal penalties aimed at people for who they are. It calls on states to protect all citizens equally under law. A rival statement drew support from other states the same day. The pair of texts shows a world split on the issue, on the record.
wild-kitty: Only the title page and a full contents list are present here for L. T. Meade's Wild Kitty, so the school tale itself does not appear. The contents open with four girls: Bessie, Alice, Gwin, and Elma. A chapter on the Blarney Stone follows. Later titles name tiffs all round, an incorrigible Kitty, and a tug-of-war. A head mistress, a lost packet, and Gwin Harley's scheme fill the middle list. The contents end with Kitty telling the truth and a lady from Buckinghamshire.
woman-in-modern-society: Earl Barnes wrote this study of women's place in modern life, copyrighted in 1912. Pages present here hold the title page, a long dedication to an ideal educated wife and mother, and part of a chapter list. The listed chapters cover what being a woman means, women's heritage, women in education, and women's pay and factory work. No chapter text itself appears in these pages.
